Mixed-Faith Marriage
mikst-fayth MAR-ij
doctrinal phrase
From mixed and faith; a marriage between a believer and an unbeliever, also called an unequal yoke.

📖 Biblical Definition

A mixed-faith marriage is a marriage between a believer and an unbeliever—a child of God joined to one outside the covenant—which Scripture forbids the believer to enter, though it instructs those already in such a marriage how to walk. The command is plain: the believer is to marry “only in the Lord,” and not to be “unequally yoked together with unbelievers,” for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness, and what communion hath light with darkness. The Old Testament warned Israel repeatedly against intermarriage with the idolatrous nations, not on grounds of race but of religion, because such unions turned the heart after other gods, as even Solomon’s wives turned away his heart. The danger is spiritual: the marriage that should be a partnership in the faith and a covenant home for godly seed becomes instead a house divided at its deepest point, with the believer pulled toward compromise and the children torn between two masters. Yet Scripture does not command the breaking of a mixed marriage already contracted; if an unbelieving spouse is content to dwell with the believer, let the believer not depart, for the unbelieving spouse is sanctified by the believing, and the believer may, by a holy walk, be the means of the other’s salvation. The dictionary holds the doctrine in both its parts: the believer is forbidden to enter a mixed-faith marriage and ought to marry only in the Lord; but the one already so married is called not to abandon the spouse, but to adorn the gospel at home and pray and hope for the other’s conversion.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A marriage between a believer and an unbeliever—the unequal yoke Scripture forbids the believer to enter, though it bids those already so married to remain and seek the spouse’s salvation.

expand to see more

MIXED-FAITH MARRIAGE, a marriage between a believer and an unbeliever.

Forbidden to enter: marry “only in the Lord,” “be ye not unequally yoked.”

The danger is spiritual—the heart turned after other gods, as Solomon’s was.

Yet the believer already so married is not to depart from a willing spouse.

The unbelieving spouse is sanctified by the believing; salvation may follow a holy walk.

📖 Key Scripture

2Co 6:14 — "Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?"

1Co 7:39 — "The wife is bound by the law as long as her husband liveth; but if her husband be dead, she is at liberty to be married to whom she will; only in the Lord."

1Co 7:13 — "And the woman which hath an husband that believeth not, and if he be pleased to dwell with her, let her not leave him."

1Ki 11:4 — "For it came to pass, when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods: and his heart was not perfect with the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The command to marry only in the Lord is dismissed as narrow, and the spiritual danger of the unequal yoke is denied.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the command to marry “only in the Lord” and not to be unequally yoked. An age that prizes romantic feeling above spiritual oneness treats this command as narrow and unloving, and counsels believers to marry where the heart inclines regardless of faith. Scripture warns otherwise: the closest of unions, when divided at its deepest point, breeds compromise in the believer and confusion in the children, as the history of Israel and of Solomon shows.

The doctrine must be guarded from a harsh misuse. Scripture forbids entering a mixed marriage but does not command breaking one already contracted; the believer married to a willing unbeliever is to remain, to walk holily, and to seek the spouse’s salvation, for the unbelieving spouse is sanctified by the believing and may be won. The dictionary holds both: a solemn warning to the unmarried to marry only in the Lord, and a tender counsel to the already-yoked believer to be faithful at home and hopeful in prayer, that the partner of the body might become a partner in the faith.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The phrase names the believer-unbeliever marriage—the unequal yoke forbidden to enter, yet to be honored where it already exists.

expand to see more

Greek heterozugeo — to be unequally yoked, joined with a different kind.

“Only in the Lord” — the limit set upon the believer’s freedom to marry.

The Old Testament warnings against intermarriage rest on religion, not race.

Greek hagiazo — to sanctify; the unbelieving spouse “sanctified” by the believing.

Solomon’s foreign wives “turned away his heart after other gods.”

Usage

"Mixed-faith marriage is taught as the unequal yoke believers are forbidden to enter."

"“Only in the Lord” guides the unmarried believer’s choice of a spouse."

"Paul’s counsel guides the believer already married to a willing unbeliever."
